title: One aluminium can, recycled, saves real energy
description: Making aluminium from raw ore takes enormous electricity. Remelting a used can takes a small fraction of it — which is why the humble drinks can is recycling's biggest success story.

body.heading: Expensive the first time
paragraphs: Aluminium begins as bauxite ore, and separating the metal takes a powerful electric process — primary aluminium is sometimes called 'solid electricity' because so much energy is locked into every ingot. Throwing a can away throws that energy away with it.

Recycling flips the maths: remelting used aluminium needs only about five percent of the energy of making it new, and the metal loses no quality in the process. A can can be recycled, refilled and back on a shelf in as little as sixty days.

body.heading: What one household does
paragraphs: Because recycled aluminium is genuinely valuable, cans are among the most recycled objects on Earth — yet billions still reach landfill each year, each one a small battery of wasted energy. Rinsing cans and keeping them in the recycling stream, never the general bin, is the whole job.
It is a rare environmental action with no downside to weigh: same metal, same can, a twentieth of the energy.

takeaway: Recycling aluminium uses about five percent of the energy of making it new, with no loss of quality — a recycled can can be back on the shelf in sixty days.
